q-71071:
We're told that $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=4.$ According to the definition of continuity, this means that ${lim}_{x\to 4}f(x)$ exists, and

$$
{lim}_{x\to 4}f(x)=f(4)=2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}{({x}^{2}-6f(x))}^{2} & ={({4}^{2}-6(2))}^{2} \\  & ={(16-12)}^{2} \\  & ={4}^{2} \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

q-149955:

The domain of $\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x-1)$ is $x\in [0,1].$ This means that $\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x-1)$ is undefined outside this interval.

Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to \,-\infty }\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(2x-1)$ is undefined.

q-128433:
The volume of the parallelepiped spanned by three vectors is given by the absolute value of their triple product.

First, we compute the triple product:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 4 \\ 3 & 9 & 2 \\ 2 & 7 & 6\end{aligned}| \\  & =0\cdot |\begin{aligned}9 & 2 \\ 7 & 6\end{aligned}|-(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}|+4\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 9 \\ 2 & 7\end{aligned}| \\  & =0+(3\cdot 6-2\cdot 2)+4(3\cdot 7-2\cdot 9) \\  & =14+12 \\  & =26\end{aligned}
$$

    

Finally, we take the absolute value. So the volume of the corresponding parallelepiped is

$$
V=|26|=26.
$$

q-73735:
Computing the triple product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot (q\times r) & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 3 & 6 \\ t & t & 2 \\ -1 & 2 & 7\end{aligned}| \\  & =0\cdot |\begin{aligned}t & 2 \\ 2 & 7\end{aligned}|-3\cdot |\begin{aligned}t & 2 \\ -1 & 7\end{aligned}|+6\cdot |\begin{aligned}t & t \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =0-3(t\cdot 7-(-1)\cdot 2)+6(t\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot t) \\  & =-21t-6+12t+6t \\  & =-3t-6.\end{aligned}
$$

    

Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their triple product is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot (q\times r) & =0 \\ -3t-6 & =0 \\ -3t & =6 \\ t & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the three vectors are coplanar if and only if $t=-2.$

q-128454:
Computing the triple product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot (q\times r) & =|\begin{aligned}t & t & 1 \\ 3 & 2 & 6 \\ 3 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =t\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 6 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}|-t\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 6 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}|+1\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}| \\  & =t(2\cdot 0-4\cdot 6)-t(3\cdot 0-3\cdot 6)+(3\cdot 4-3\cdot 2) \\  & =-24t+18t+6 \\  & =-6t+6 \\  & =6(1-t).\end{aligned}
$$

    

Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their triple product is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot (q\times r) & =0 \\ 6(1-t) & =0 \\ 1-t & =0 \\ t & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the three vectors are coplanar if and only if $t=1.$

q-128483:
First, we find the displacement vectors $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ that span the parallelepiped:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =(4i+j+7k)-(5i+j+4k) \\  & =-i+3k \\  & =⟨-1,0,3⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =(3i+j+5k)-(5i+j+4k) \\  & =-2i+k \\  & =⟨-2,0,1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AD} & =d-a \\  & =(2i+3j+3k)-(5i+j+4k) \\  & =-3i+2j-k \\  & =⟨-3,2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the volume of the parallelepiped, we need to take the absolute value of the triple product of the above vectors.

Computing the triple product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot (\overset{\to }{AC}\times \overset{\to }{AD}) & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 3 \\ -2 & 0 & 1 \\ -3 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|-0\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}|+3\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(0\cdot (-1)-2\cdot 1)-0+3((-2)\cdot 2-(-3)\cdot 0) \\  & =2-12 \\  & =-10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the corresponding parallelepiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ is

$$
V=|-10|=10.
$$

q-128475:
First, we find the displacement vectors $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ that span the parallelepiped:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =(8i+5j+9k)-(7i+6j+4k) \\  & =i-j+5k \\  & =⟨1,-1,5⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =(7i+4j+2k)-(7i+6j+4k) \\  & =-2j-2k \\  & =⟨0,-2,-2⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AD} & =d-a \\  & =(5i+7j+4k)-(7i+6j+4k) \\  & =-2i+j \\  & =⟨-2,1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the volume of the parallelepiped, we need to take the absolute value of the triple product of the above vectors.

Computing the triple product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot (\overset{\to }{AC}\times \overset{\to }{AD}) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 5 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|-(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}|+5\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =((-2)\cdot 0-1\cdot (-2))+(0\cdot 0-(-2)\cdot (-2))+5(0\cdot 1-(-2)\cdot (-2)) \\  & =2-4-20 \\  & =-22.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the corresponding parallelepiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ is

$$
V=|-22|=22.
$$

q-73064:
**Step 1:** First, we write the inverse function implicitly. The given function is $y=3{x}^{3}+9x,$ and to write the inverse function implicitly, we swap $x$ and $y$ as follows:

$$
x=3{y}^{3}+9y
$$

Note that in the equation above, we have $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

**Step 2:** Next, we differentiate. The overall goal is to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ but the equation is already solved for $x,$ so we compute $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}$ and then take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(3{y}^{3}+9y) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =9{y}^{2}+9 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{9{y}^{2}+9}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3:** Lastly, we write the result in terms of ${f}^{-1}(x).$ Since $y={f}^{-1}(x),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[{f}^{-1}(x)] & =\frac{1}{9{({f}^{-1}(x))}^{2}+9} \\ {({f}^{-1})}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{9{({f}^{-1}(x))}^{2}+9}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-110046:
**Step 1:** First, we write the inverse function implicitly. The given function is $y=8{x}^{6}+4{x}^{4}+3{x}^{3}-12,$ and to write the inverse function implicitly, we swap $x$ and $y$ as follows:

$$
x=8{y}^{6}+4{y}^{4}+3{y}^{3}-12
$$

Note that in the equation above, we have $y={h}^{-1}(x).$

**Step 2:** Next, we differentiate. The overall goal is to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ but the equation is already solved for $x,$ so we compute $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y}$ and then take the reciprocal:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(8{y}^{6}+4{y}^{4}+3{y}^{3}-12) \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =48{y}^{5}+16{y}^{3}+9{y}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{48{y}^{5}+16{y}^{3}+9{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3:** Lastly, we write the result in terms of ${h}^{-1}(x).$ Since $y={h}^{-1}(x),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[{h}^{-1}(x)] & =\frac{1}{48({h}^{-1}(x))^{5}+16({h}^{-1}(x))^{3}+9({h}^{-1}(x))^{2}} \\ {({h}^{-1})}^{′}(x) & =\frac{1}{48({h}^{-1}(x))^{5}+16({h}^{-1}(x))^{3}+9({h}^{-1}(x))^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-127913:
First, we find the vectors $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ and $\overset{\to }{PR}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =q-p \\  & =(5i+j+7k)-(6i+j+5k) \\  & =-i+2k \\  & =⟨-1,0,2⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{PR} & =r-p \\  & =(4i+2j)-(6i+j+5k) \\  & =-2i+j-5k \\  & =⟨-2,1,-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the formula to compute the cross product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ}\times \overset{\to }{PR} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -1 & 0 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & -5\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & -5\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -2 & -5\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(0\cdot (-5)-1\cdot 2)i-((-1)\cdot (-5)-(-2)\cdot 2)j+((-1)\cdot 1-(-2)\cdot 0)k \\  & =-2i-9j-k \\  & =⟨-2,-9,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ and $\overset{\to }{PR}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\overset{\to }{PQ}\times \overset{\to }{PR}| \\  & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-9)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{86}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $△\,PQR$ is

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}A=\frac{\sqrt{86}}{2}.
$$

q-20027:
Note that the length of the altitude $CH$ can be related to the area of $△\,ABC$ as follows:

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}CH\cdot AB
$$

So, to find $CH,$ we first find ${A}_{△}.$ To start, we find the vectors $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =(i+2j+k)-(2i+j+2k) \\  & =-i+j-k \\  & =⟨-1,1,-1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =(3i+2j+3k)-(2i+j+2k) \\  & =i+j+k \\  & =⟨1,1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\times \overset{\to }{AC} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(1\cdot 1-1\cdot (-1))i-((-1)\cdot 1-1\cdot (-1))j+((-1)\cdot 1-1\cdot 1)k \\  & =2i-2k \\  & =⟨2,0,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB}$ and $\overset{\to }{AC}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|\overset{\to }{AB}\times \overset{\to }{AC}| \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{8} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The area of the triangle is half of the area of the respective parallelogram. So, the area of $△\,ABC$ is

$$
{A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}A=\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{2}=\sqrt{2}.
$$

Let's also compute $AB$ since it appears in the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =|\overset{\to }{AB}| \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, using the formula ${A}_{△}=\frac{1}{2}CH\cdot AB,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{△} & =\frac{1}{2}CH\cdot AB \\ \sqrt{2} & =\frac{1}{2}CH\cdot \sqrt{3} \\ 2\sqrt{2} & =CH\cdot \sqrt{3} \\ CH & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ CH & =\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-89660:
Since ${4}^{x}+{x}^{2}$ is always positive, we can divide both sides of the inequality by this quantity. By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{({4}^{x}+{x}^{2})(2x-3)}{{4}^{x}+{x}^{2}} & \ge \frac{0}{{4}^{x}+{x}^{2}} \\ 2x-3 & \ge 0 \\ 2x & \ge 3 \\ x & \ge \frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-21035:
For continuous, twice-differentiable functions, we can determine possible points of inflection by solving the equation ${f}^{″}(x)=0.$ However, we must be sure to check that the concavity does indeed change at whatever points we find.

First, we calculate the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =12-\frac{3}{{x}^{2}} \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =\frac{6}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we solve ${f}^{″}(x)=0:$ 

$$
\frac{6}{{x}^{3}}=0
$$

The equation above has no real solutions, so there are no points of inflection.

q-31213:
First, notice that since $f(x)$ is twice-differentiable, the tangent line to the graph exists for all real $x.$

Inflection points occur when a graph changes concavity. In order for the graph to change concavity, the value of the second derivative ${f}^{″}(x)$ must switch sign. So, we are looking for points where the graph of ${f}^{″}(x)$ crosses the $x$-axis.

We can see that the graph $y={f}^{″}(x)$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x=0$ and $x=4.$ 

Therefore, $f(x)$ has points of inflection at $x=0$ and $x=4.$

q-4772:
First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+3t) \\  & =2t+3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+3) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the acceleration at time $t=10,$ we substitute this into the above:

$$
a(10)=2\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}
$$

Therefore, the acceleration when $t=10$ seconds is $2\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$
